label: unrelated
point: The Court held that an FLSA administrative subpoena for required payroll records may be enforced without a prior judicial warrant; it did not construe 12 U.S.C. 3414.
change: The law rewrote the Right to Financial Privacy Act's nondisclosure rules in 3414(a)(3) and (a)(5)(D) and updated a Secret Service cross-reference.
why: The committee report cites Lone Steer only as general background on administrative subpoenas; the changes to the financial-privacy nondisclosure rules have nothing to do with the decision's Fourth Amendment holding.

label: codifies
point: Wickard held that Congress may regulate purely local activity that in the aggregate substantially affects interstate commerce; it did not concern 18 U.S.C. 116.
change: The law rewrote the FGM offense in 116(a), raised the maximum penalty to 10 years, broadened the no-defense rule in (c), and added interstate or foreign commerce circumstances in a new (d).
why: The committee report relies on Wickard's aggregation principle, with approval, as the basis for the new commerce element, so Congress builds on the decision rather than departing from it; the decision never applied 116 itself.

label: override_express
point: The court held that the contingent-fee portion of an age-discrimination settlement is gross income to the client, so the fee is only a miscellaneous itemized deduction that is disallowed for the alternative minimum tax.
change: The shown 26 U.S.C. 1 changes only drop foreign investment company references, but the same Act (AJCA 2004) added an above-the-line deduction for attorney fees in unlawful-discrimination claims, with a report that names Kenseth among the cases at issue.
why: The new deduction would let a Kenseth-type age-discrimination claimant deduct the fee for AMT purposes, reversing the decision's tax result, and the report names the case; the gross-income inclusion itself is left in place, and the change sits outside the shown section 1 text.

label: codifies
point: The court disregarded Heinz's stock-redemption loss transaction under the sham-transaction and economic-substance doctrine, applying a test that fails a transaction lacking either economic substance or a non-tax purpose.
change: The shown 26 U.S.C. 105 change only extends tax-free medical reimbursement to children under 27; the same Act codified the economic substance doctrine with a conjunctive objective-and-subjective test.
why: The report lists Heinz among the cases applying the economic substance doctrine that the Act writes into the Code, consistent with the decision's approach; the section 105 change itself is unrelated.

label: unrelated
point: The court held that a permanent resident cannot count earlier unlawful presence toward the seven-year lawful domicile required for 212(c) relief; 28 U.S.C. 1404 played no part.
change: The law allowed transfer under 1404(a) to any district all parties consent to and barred transfers to the territorial district courts.
why: The report cites the case only for the meaning of lawful domicile in the general venue provision; the 1404 transfer changes have nothing to do with the decision.

label: codifies
point: The Tenth Circuit addressed the Secretary's acceptance of the downtown Kansas City tract in trust for the Wyandotte Tribe and gaming on it under IGRA; it did not involve the National Trails System Act.
change: The shown change adds a Captain John Smith Chesapeake watertrail study to 16 U.S.C. 1244(c); separately, Sec. 119 of the Act states that a 2002 appropriations provision does not affect the Sac and Fox Nation v. Norton decision.
why: The law names the decision only to preserve it against an earlier rider, so Congress leaves the decision's holding intact; the trail-study amendment to 1244 is itself unrelated.

label: related
point: The court held that Long Term's tax opinions did not establish the reasonable cause and good faith defense under 26 U.S.C. 6664(c)(1), and it sustained the valuation and understatement penalties.
change: The law added 6664(c)(2), which denies the reasonable cause exception for underpayments from transactions lacking economic substance under 6662(b)(6), and renumbered the following paragraphs.
why: The amendment narrows the same defense on the same subject but only makes the decision's result (no reasonable cause relief) more certain; it does not reverse the rule the court applied, and the report cites the case only as an economic-substance precedent.

label: related
point: The Federal Circuit held that it lacked jurisdiction over the claim that the Veterans Court, under 38 U.S.C. 7261, affirmed on a ground the Board did not use, and it held that VCAA section 3(a) does not apply retroactively.
change: The law amended 7261 to require the Veterans Court to review the record, take due account of the benefit-of-the-doubt rule, and set aside or reverse clearly erroneous findings adverse to the claimant.
why: The 7261 changes alter the standard and scope of Veterans Court review on the same subject, but they do not reach the decision's jurisdictional ruling or its VCAA non-retroactivity holding, which the report cites only as background.

label: unrelated
point: The en banc Seventh Circuit applied the amended 28 U.S.C. 2254(d) to pending cases, noting only in passing that habeas subject-matter jurisdiction survives under 2241.
change: The Military Commissions Act rewrote 2241(e) to strip habeas and related jurisdiction over aliens detained as enemy combatants or awaiting that determination.
why: The report cites the Supreme Court decision in Lindh (521 U.S. 320) on whether jurisdiction-stripping applies to pending cases, but the 2241(e) detainee provisions have nothing to do with this decision's passing cite of 2241.

label: related
point: The Federal Circuit held that a VCAA 5103(a) notice error is presumed prejudicial, so the VA must show the error was harmless.
change: The law added 5103(a)(2), directing the Secretary to prescribe by regulation the contents of notice by claim type, including generic information on the elements of each type of claim.
why: The report names Simmons among the concerns behind the amendment, but the law addresses the content of the notice rather than the prejudice presumption or burden the decision adopted; that rule was later displaced by the Supreme Court in Shinseki v. Sanders, not by this statute.
